inputs.original_text: Tens of thousands marched in central London under the banner of opposing the “far-right,” with trade unions, anti-racism groups and Muslim representative bodies among the organisers. With local elections approaching, this looks less like a neutral show of civic concern and more like organised pressure to define which views are acceptable. Calling people “far-right” is an easy way to dismiss concerns about national identity, social order and cultural continuity instead of answering them. Tradition and public debate deserve better than political labels.
inputs.modified_text: Tens of thousands marched in central London under an “anti-far-right” banner, backed by trade unions, anti-racism groups and Muslim representative bodies. With local elections approaching, the timing looks like an effort to set the boundaries of acceptable opinion before voters have their say. Branding dissent as “far-right” is no substitute for answering people’s concerns about national identity, social order and the traditions that bind communities together. A healthy society should defend open debate, not use political labels to shut it down.
